justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I would have assessed as a recent baseline level around 300–305 for the underlying asset or metric in question. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 304 assumes very little net movement from the prevailing level, consistent with mean-reverting short-term dynamics and no imminent scheduled catalysts. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 306, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption that is common when markets or series are trending modestly upward without strong reversal signals. At the one-month horizon, 310 represents a continuation of that gentle upward bias, compounded over more time steps but still anchored near current levels given the inherent uncertainty over longer horizons.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately with the forecast horizon, reflecting the well-established principle that uncertainty accumulates over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 11 points around the estimate is driven primarily by normal short-term volatility — intraday or day-to-day fluctuations that are relatively predictable in magnitude. At one week, the interval expands to roughly plus or minus 22 points, incorporating the possibility of several consecutive moves in one direction, news surprises, or shifts in sentiment. By one month, the interval of roughly plus or minus 42 points accounts for a full range of potential macro developments, trend reversals, and compounding volatility over approximately 20 trading sessions.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden macro shocks such as unexpected central bank policy announcements, geopolitical escalations, or significant economic data surprises that could produce outsized single-day moves well beyond the one-day interval. At the monthly horizon, a broader regime change — such as a sharp deterioration in credit conditions, an equity market correction, or a commodity supply disruption — could plausibly push outcomes far beyond the stated bounds. Liquidity crises or black swan events are by definition poorly captured by standard volatility-based intervals.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly normally distributed or log-normally distributed outcomes with relatively stable volatility. In reality, volatility itself is stochastic and can cluster — a period of calm can give way abruptly to elevated turbulence, which would widen the true distribution of outcomes beyond what my stated intervals suggest. If the asset or metric has meaningful skew or kurtosis in its historical distribution, the downside tail in particular may be fatter than my symmetric confidence intervals imply.
